newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan tones down weak yen policy.
newsitem.headline: Japan tones down weak yen policy.

text.p: Japan apparently toned down its policy of seeking a weaker yen on Thursday, but the move was unlikely to impede the dollar's gains over the long term, currency dealers say.

Comments by influential Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara put the brakes on the dollar's recent rally, the first time he has said anything remotely negative about the dollar's rise since he became involved in driving the dollar up from its post-war global low against the yen in August 1995.

Currency dealers said Sakakibara's remarks did not imply a complete reversal of a strong dollar, but gave a signal that an excessive dollar rise was not desirable if it was not justified by fundamentals.
"We are closely watching current developments in the currency market," Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, told reporters.
Sakakibara, dubbed "Mr Yen" by the foreign media, is said to be the key figure in driving the dollar above 100 yen last year through aggressive government intervention in foreign exchange markets.
The dollar fell to a low of 112.01 yen from 113.80 yen in Tokyo trade, following Sakakibara's remarks. It was standing at 111.80 yen in European trade.

"(The Ministry of Finance) wanted to slow down the tempo of the dollar's rally, although it still hopes to steadily lift the dollar," said Noriyuki Mizukami, head of treasury sales at National Westminster Bank in Tokyo.
Larry Duke, vice president, Citibank, Tokyo, agreed.
"I don't think it changes the bullish trend for the dollar, though the rate of its appreciation could be slower than the market had thought before," he said.
"Monetary authorities in both the United States and Japan will be happy with a dollar rate of 105-115 yen," he added.
Sakakibara also said the market view of Japan's economy was too pessimistic and that he believed it was stronger than the market believed.
Dealers said Sakakibara comments were timely, coming right after the U.S. presidential election.

Dealers had refrained from selling dollars as the U.S. government apparently wanted a strong dollar because a falling dollar might have hurt U.S. stock and bonds and affected Bill Clinton's re-election bid.
A senior MOF official said later on Thursday that there had been no change in the ministry's stance on currencies due to any special factors.
Dealers said the dollar could come under further selling pressure against the yen soon, but was unlikely to fall below 110 yen because of extremely low interest rates in Japan.
The low interest rates have been the major cause behind the yen's steep slide as they have caused investors to unload yen for higher-yielding overseas assets.
The dollar's recent surge pushed it up to a 42-month high of 114.92 yen in Tokyo last week, a 44 percent rebound from its post-war global low of 79.75 yen set in mid-April 1995.

The stronger yen hurts Japanese exporters by making their products more expensive overseas, but Japanese business leaders have recently voiced concern about the rise in the dollar, as it increases the cost of materials and products they import.
